rules.statement: When a credential store has no password hash it can verify for the submitted user name (no account, no password, locked-out user, or an unreadable stored hash), verify the submitted password against a dummy hash made with the current hashing parameters, through the same code path used for a stored hash, and then refuse the password whatever the result.
rules.why: OWASP ASVS V6.3.8 says valid users must not be deducible from response times. A path that skips the expensive hash verification answers much sooner and shows that the account exists.
rules.check: Look for early returns in sign-in, password-grant or password-change lookups that fail without running a hash verification when the user is missing, has no password, is locked out or has a malformed hash. Also look for a dummy verification whose success could let the request through.

rules.statement: Verify the stored hash, or the dummy hash when there is none, with a single call to the verifier (for example `VerifyHashedPassword(storedHash ?? dummyHash, password)`) instead of putting the dummy and real verifications on separate branches.
rules.why: A single call guarantees that every path costs the same number of hash verifications.
rules.check: Look for if/else branches that call the password verifier differently, or a different number of times, depending on whether an account or hash was found.

rules.statement: A password hasher that finds a stored hash it cannot parse should do the work of verifying the dummy hash before it reports failure, rather than failing right away.
rules.why: Otherwise a damaged or foreign hash can be told apart by how quickly the hasher fails.
rules.check: Look for format or parse checks in the hash verifier that return failure without first running a derivation of the dummy hash.

rules.statement: Build the dummy password hash once, ahead of time (for example in a constructor or a singleton, and before the user lookup). Use the hasher's own format and current parameters, with a random salt and a random key or password, so that no known password matches it and verifying against it costs the same as verifying a real current hash.
rules.why: A dummy built lazily on first use, or with other parameters, would make the first or the dummy verification cost a different amount than a real one, which leaks whether the account exists.
rules.check: Look for dummy hashes that are hard-coded or guessable, use other iterations or sizes than the current settings, or are created lazily inside the failure path after the lookup.

rules.statement: Run every step used for a stored hash when verifying against the dummy hash as well, including any retry with a normalized form of the password (such as NFC first, then the password as submitted), so a wrong password costs the same number of hash verifications on every path.
rules.why: If the dummy path skipped a step, it would take fewer verifications, and the timing difference would reveal that the account does not exist.
rules.check: Look for normalization fallbacks or extra verification attempts that run only when a real stored hash exists.

rules.statement: In tests of timing-safe credential verification, assert that the dummy hash was verified (for example through a fake or spy hasher) instead of measuring elapsed time.
rules.why: Elapsed time is flaky when tests run in parallel.
rules.check: Look for tests that use Stopwatch or compare durations to prove that verification takes constant time.
